# Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-efficiency}

**On HiLiftAeroML, GeoTransolver and Transolver match or beat ISLA at every
training-set size measured.** With every architecture fed the freestream as
a unit direction, GeoTransolver's surface-pressure error is 0.72x of the
ISLA reference configuration's at 35 training cases, 0.75x at 210, 0.75x at
4 training geometries, 0.87x at 21 and 0.68x at a fixed angle of attack;
Transolver's is 0.75x, 0.81x, 0.77x, 0.88x and 0.75x on the same rungs.
Against ISLA's constant-gauge variant the ratios run 0.76–0.92x for
GeoTransolver and 0.77–0.93x for Transolver, including 0.84x and 0.90x at
510 cases, where that variant is the only ISLA. The 1,260-case rung has no
unit-drive baseline and is not yet measured as a comparison. What stands
about ISLA alone is that its error responds to the number of distinct
training geometries, tracks the flow physics case by case, and comes with a
usable per-case uncertainty signal from 35 cases. On DrivAerML the ordering
is the same: GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate than ISLA from 27
training cars up (@sec-de-drivaerml). Every ratio between architectures in
this book is the baseline's error divided by ISLA's, so a value above one
favours ISLA; the metric is the cell-area-weighted relative L2 of surface
pressure, a surface integral (@sec-metrics). The chapter's limits are in
@sec-de-limits and collected with the rest of the book's in @sec-limits.

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Its
curated data-efficiency splits are nested, 35 training cases inside 210
inside 510 inside 1,260, and all four share one 180-case validation set and
one sealed 360-case test set (@sec-splits). The training subsets are random
draws from the 1,260-case pool, so the 35-case split contains 3–7 cases at
each angle except 18°, of which it has none, and 33 distinct geometries.
Two further ladders vary what the training set contains rather than how
large it is: a geometry ladder of 40 cases on 4 geometries and 210 cases on
21 geometries, each at all ten angles and validated on 180 cases of 18
geometries that appear in no training set, and a fixed-angle split of 126
geometries at 12°, validated on 18 held-out geometries at the same angle.

The quantity reported is the relative L2 error of surface pressure on the
validation cases (@sec-metrics): for one case, the cell-area-weighted norm
of the error over its 10,000 sampled surface points divided by the
same norm of the true field, then the arithmetic mean over the cases. Every
architecture is trained under the frozen protocol (@sec-protocol): 10,000
sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16 training, no
augmentation, two or three seeds, and the learning rate each architecture
prefers on the full split (1e-3 for ISLA; 3e-3 for Transolver; 1e-3 for
GeoTransolver, except at 35 cases, where its 3e-3 lane is better and is the
one reported). Every number in this chapter is a float32 evaluation of the
final-epoch checkpoint; no checkpoint is selected on validation error
(@sec-metrics for the reporting instrument). Resources are matched in
parameters (8.9M for ISLA against 9.0M for GeoTransolver and 6.0M for
Transolver) and in tokens per case; at 10,000 tokens on one GB300 the
compiled ISLA step is 47 ms in 1.30 GiB against GeoTransolver's 45 ms in
2.70 GiB (@sec-cost). The validation set was used for the learning-rate
choice on the full split, for the per-rung learning-rate choice of the
baselines, and, as in any sequential program, by ablations designed after
earlier readouts and by the selection of what to present (@sec-de-limits).
The sealed test split was never read by any model in this chapter.

Every architecture receives the freestream as a unit direction. This is a
protocol requirement, not a convenience: fed the physical freestream
velocity of 2,679.5 in/s instead, GeoTransolver's global-context projector
collapses to one occupied slice per head and both baselines lose 3.4–3.8x
at 35 cases. The mechanism, the control that established it and the
resulting rule are in @sec-part-baseline; the numbers in this chapter are
the unit-drive ones.

ISLA appears in two configurations. The reference configuration is the
relative frame with the total-measure scale (@sec-mt2): no centroid, no
sample-estimated length, translation invariance from point-to-anchor
vectors alone. The constant-gauge variant centres on the plain mean of the
sampled points and uses a constant reference length. The reference exists
on the 35-case, 210-case, 4-geometry, 21-geometry and fixed-angle rungs;
at 510 and 1,260 cases the constant-gauge variant is the only ISLA, and the
tables say so.

## The ladder {#sec-de-result}

**Both unit-drive baselines are more accurate than ISLA on every rung:
baseline ÷ ISLA lies between 0.68 and 0.88 against the reference
configuration and between 0.76 and 0.93 against the constant-gauge
variant.** @fig-hilift-data-efficiency and
@tbl-hilift-ladder show the three ladders side by side.

```{python}

import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, BLUE2, RED, AMBER = "#2a78d6", "#7fb0e6", "#e34948", "#c98a2b"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
RES = Path("..") / "results"
fp = json.load(open(RES / "fp32_reeval" / "fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json"))["runs"]
fr = json.load(open(RES / "frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json"))["hilift_val"]
u210 = json.load(open(RES / "udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json"))["three_seed_addendum_fp32"]
u510 = json.load(open(RES / "udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json"))["arms_fp32"]
g210 = json.load(open(RES / "geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json"))["arms_fp32"]
fa = json.load(open(RES / "now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json"))["arms_fp32"]
def fp32(prefix, seeds):
    return [fp[f"{prefix}_seed{s}"]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for s in seeds if f"{prefix}_seed{s}" in fp]
def frame(prefix, seeds=(42, 43, 44)):
    return [fr[f"{prefix}_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in seeds if f"{prefix}_seed{s}" in fr]
# rung -> arm -> list of per-seed float32 pressure rel-L2
LADDER = {
 "35 cases": {"gt": fp32("udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3", (42, 43)),
              "t": fp32("udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3", (42, 43, 44)),
              "isla": frame("rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce"),
              "cg": fp32("lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce", (42, 43, 44))},
 "210 cases": {"gt": u210["gt_unit_lr1e3"]["seed_pressure"], "t": u210["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"],
               "isla": frame("rf_hl_mt2_meas_scarce"), "cg": fp32("lad_hl_mt2_scarce", (42, 43, 44)) or [u210["isla"]["pressure_l2"]]},
 "510 cases": {"gt": u510["gt_unit"]["seed_pressure"], "t": u510["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"],
               "isla": [], "cg": u510["isla_prior"]["seed_pressure"]},
 "4 geometries": {"gt": fp32("udrv_hl_gt_geometry_super_scarce", (42, 43)),
                  "t": fp32("udrv_hl_transolver_geometry_super_scarce_lr3e3", (42, 43)),
                  "isla": frame("rf_hl_mt2_meas_geometry_super_scarce"),
                  "cg": fp32("geo_hl_mt2_geometry_super_scarce", (42, 43))},
 "21 geometries": {"gt": g210["gt_unit"]["seed_pressure"], "t": g210["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"],
                   "isla": frame("rf_hl_mt2_meas_geometry_scarce"), "cg": g210["isla_weights_on"]["seed_pressure"]},
 "fixed angle": {"gt": fa["gt_unit"]["seed_pressure"], "t": fa["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"],
                 "isla": frame("rf_hl_mt2_meas_single_aoa_12"), "cg": fa["isla_weights_on"]["seed_pressure"]},
}
STYLE = {"gt": ("GeoTransolver", RED, "o", "-"), "t": ("Transolver", AMBER, "^", "-"),
         "isla": ("ISLA, reference configuration", BLUE, "s", "-"),
         "cg": ("ISLA, constant-gauge variant", BLUE2, "D", "--")}
PANELS = [("Random splits, 180 validation cases", [("35 cases", 35), ("210 cases", 210), ("510 cases", 510)], "Training cases [count]", "log"),
          ("Never-seen geometries, 180 validation cases", [("4 geometries", 4), ("21 geometries", 21)], "Training geometries [count]", "log"),
          ("Fixed angle (12°), 18 held-out geometries", [("fixed angle", 126)], "Training geometries [count]", "linear")]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.0, 4.8), sharey=True, gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 2.2, 1.2]})
for ax, (title, rungs, xlabel, xscale) in zip(axs, PANELS):
    for arm, (label, c, mk, ls) in STYLE.items():
        xs, ys = [], []
        for name, x in rungs:
            v = LADDER[name][arm]
            if not v:
                continue
            xs.append(x); ys.append(statistics.mean(v))
            ax.scatter([x] * len(v), v, color=c, s=12, alpha=0.9, zorder=4)
        if xs:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=c, lw=1.8, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, mfc="white", mec=c, mew=1.6, zorder=3,
                    label=label if ax is axs[0] else None)
    ax.set_xscale(xscale); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ticks = [x for _, x in rungs]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks); ax.set_xticklabels([f"{x:,}" for x in ticks])
    if xscale == "log":
        ax.set_xlim(ticks[0] / 1.6, ticks[-1] * 1.6)
    else:
        ax.set_xlim(ticks[0] - 40, ticks[0] + 40)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel, color=INK2)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=9.5, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
axs[0].set_yticks([0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
axs[0].set_yticklabels(["0.03", "0.05", "0.10", "0.20", "0.30"])
axs[0].set_ylim(0.024, 0.32)
axs[0].set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]  (float32, log)", color=INK2)
fig.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=4, fontsize=8.8, bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 0.995), handlelength=2.4, columnspacing=1.4)
fig.suptitle("HiLiftAeroML ladders: unit-drive baselines against ISLA (points: seeds; lines: seed means)",
             x=0.01, y=0.925, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=10.5)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.9))
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import statistics
def cell(v):
    if not v:
        return "not trained"
    m = statistics.mean(v)
    return f"{m:.4f} ({min(v):.4f}–{max(v):.4f})" if len(v) > 1 else f"{m:.4f}"
def ratio(a, b):
    return f"{statistics.mean(a) / statistics.mean(b):.2f}" if a and b else "—"
print("| rung | GeoTransolver | Transolver | ISLA, reference | ISLA, constant-gauge variant | GT ÷ ISLA ref | T ÷ ISLA ref | GT ÷ ISLA const | T ÷ ISLA const |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
for name in ("35 cases", "210 cases", "510 cases", "4 geometries", "21 geometries", "fixed angle"):
    r = LADDER[name]
    print(f"| {name} | {cell(r['gt'])} | {cell(r['t'])} | **{cell(r['isla'])}** | {cell(r['cg'])} | "
          f"{ratio(r['gt'], r['isla'])} | {ratio(r['t'], r['isla'])} | {ratio(r['gt'], r['cg'])} | {ratio(r['t'], r['cg'])} |")
print()
print(": The HiLiftAeroML ladders in float32: seed mean (seed range) of surface-pressure relative L2 on the shared validation cases, and each baseline's mean divided by each ISLA configuration's mean (below 1 means the baseline is more accurate). GeoTransolver at learning rate 3e-3 at 35 cases and 1e-3 elsewhere; Transolver at 3e-3; ISLA at 1e-3. The reference configuration is the relative frame with the total-measure scale; the constant-gauge variant is the only ISLA trained at 510 cases. Same sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

Along the case ladder the ratio against the constant-gauge variant is flat:
GeoTransolver 0.80x, 0.84x and 0.84x at 35, 210 and 510 cases, Transolver
0.83x, 0.90x and 0.90x. Per case the same ordering holds: at 210 cases
GeoTransolver is lower than the constant-gauge ISLA on 161 of 180
validation cases and Transolver on 149; at 510 both are lower on 168 of
180; at 21 geometries on 136 and 135 of 180; at the fixed angle both are
lower on all 18 held-out geometries (median per-geometry ISLA ÷
GeoTransolver 1.24, ISLA ÷ Transolver 1.13, exact sign test p = 8 × 10⁻⁶).
At 4 geometries the mean and the count disagree: GeoTransolver is 0.76x by
the mean but lower on only 96 of 180 cases and 9 of 18 geometries (median
per-geometry ratio 1.03, 10–90% range 0.78–2.06), because a tail of
geometries on which ISLA is up to twice as bad carries the mean
(results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json,
results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json,
results/now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json; verdicts @sec-nb-udrvl-210-verdict,
@sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict, @sec-nb-geo210-arms-verdict,
@sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict, @sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict). The
preregistered bars for the ladder (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg) placed an ISLA
advantage at baseline ÷ ISLA ≥ 1.10 with ISLA lower on two thirds of the
cases; no rung approaches them. At 35 cases the baselines lead on velocity
and wall shear as well as pressure (GeoTransolver 0.136 and 0.210,
Transolver 0.141 and 0.217, against 0.168 and 0.256 for the constant-gauge
ISLA; results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json), and at the fixed angle
likewise (0.052 and 0.083, 0.057 and 0.094, against 0.064 and 0.104).

**The reference configuration pays for carrying no mesher information, and
the price depends on whether validation geometries recur in training.** On
the rungs where the reference exists its error against the constant-gauge
variant is +11% at 35 cases (0.1529 against 0.1377), +11% at 210 (0.0716
against 0.0643), +1% at 4 geometries (0.2520 against 0.2496), +5% at 21
(0.1066 against 0.1014) and +14.4% at the fixed angle (0.0398 against
0.0348, three seeds); on DrivAerML it is free (0.0552 against 0.0557,
@sec-full-data-accuracy). The two random-split rungs, where the validation
geometries appear in training at other angles, pay 11%; the never-seen
geometry rungs pay 1–5%. On the 35-case and fixed-angle splits, where a
diagnostic ISLA was given the exact frame of the full geometry as global
data, it paid as much or more (+14–16% and +21%), so the price is not
positional information lost with the frame; it is the pattern the plain-mean
centroid reads from the mesher's cell placement, which displaces the centre
by 0.131 body lengths on these wings and by 0.034 on DrivAerML cars
(results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json; @sec-nb-frame-full-verdict,
@sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict, @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict).
That content is discretization-dependent and the reference does not carry
it (@sec-principle); the consistency benchmark of @sec-consistency-bench is
where the reference earns its price.

**How much of the 35-case ordering belongs to the particular 35 cases? None
of it, but the two-seed spreads understate the uncertainty.** The 35-case
split is one random draw from the 1,260-case pool. Re-running
GeoTransolver, Transolver and the constant-gauge ISLA on three further
geometry-stratified 35-case draws, three seeds each, gives GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA of 0.881, 0.892 and 0.957 against 0.895 on the curated draw at
learning rate 1e-3 (mean 0.910, 90% interval 0.84–0.98) and Transolver ÷
ISLA of 0.846, 0.852 and 0.900 against 0.829 (mean 0.866, interval
0.82–0.92); the ordering holds on every draw, and the curated draw is
typical for every arm
(`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json`).
The between-draw standard deviation of an arm's error is 8.8
(GeoTransolver), 10.9 (Transolver) and 3.4 (ISLA, whose seed spread is two
to three times the others') times its between-seed standard deviation, and
the hardest draw is 24% harder than the easiest for GeoTransolver. A
two-seed number at this rung therefore understates its uncertainty by a
factor of 3–11, and every 35-case ratio in this book is to be read with the
intervals above. At 210 cases the same design gives GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA
0.873 (interval 0.82–0.93) and Transolver ÷ ISLA 0.903 (0.85–0.95), with
between-draw to between-seed ratios of 1.8–3.1 for ISLA and GeoTransolver
and 7.6 for Transolver, whose seeds nearly coincide
(`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json`).
The two baselines trade places with data: GeoTransolver's lead grows from
35 to 210 cases (0.91 to 0.87) while Transolver's shrinks (0.87 to 0.90).

The 1,260-case rung is the one place the ladder is incomplete. The
constant-gauge ISLA scores 0.041 there (two seeds 0.040 / 0.043;
results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json), its curve running 0.138,
0.065, 0.049, 0.041 with log-log slopes 0.42, 0.31 and 0.21 over the three
segments; neither unit-drive baseline nor the reference configuration is
trained at this rung, so the full-split comparison on HiLiftAeroML is not
yet measured (@sec-program-status).

## Controls {#sec-de-controls}

The baselines were given every steel-man the protocol allows. Learning
rate: at 35 cases GeoTransolver at 3e-3 (0.1102, two seeds 0.1117 / 0.1089)
beats its 1e-3 lane (0.1232, three seeds) on 158 of 180 cases, so the
protocol's best-rate rule reports 3e-3 there and 1e-3 at every other rung;
Transolver at 1e-3 is worse than at 3e-3 at 35 cases (0.1266 against
0.1142) and stays at 3e-3 (results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json,
@sec-nb-wave3-35-verdict). Seeds: third seeds at 35 cases move neither
baseline's mean by more than 0.001, and the 210-case third seeds move
GeoTransolver from 0.0533 to 0.0539 and Transolver from 0.0582 to 0.0578
(@sec-nb-udrvl-210-seed44). Draws: the three further 35-case and 210-case
draws above. Measure: giving GeoTransolver and Transolver the same
quadrature measure ISLA carries, in their slice pooling, costs them 6.5% at
35 cases (0.1173 and 0.1217, three seeds) and leaves them at 0.85x and
0.88x of the constant-gauge ISLA; these measure-weighted baselines are
research variants that locate a property, not modifications of the
released models (@sec-nb-mw-verdict, @sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines).
ISLA's own controls are the single-factor ablations of @sec-mechanism.

## What ISLA's error responds to {#sec-de-strata}

**ISLA's error is paid for in geometries, not cases, and it tracks the flow
physics case by case; the deficit to the baselines is representational.**
Three facts about ISLA alone stand independent of any baseline.

*Geometry count.* Trained on 40 cases made of four geometries at all ten
angles, the constant-gauge ISLA reaches 0.2496 and the reference 0.2520,
against 0.1377 and 0.1529 from 35 cases on 33 geometries; on 210 cases
from 21 geometries 0.1014 and 0.1066 against 0.0643 and 0.0716 from 210
cases on about 126 geometries. Cutting the training geometries six- to
eight-fold at a similar case count costs ISLA 1.5–1.8x. The comparison
changes two things at once, the training composition and the evaluation
population (the random-split and geometry-ladder validation sets share only
20 of 180 cases), so it supports a geometry-count reading and not the
stronger statement that geometry count alone sets ISLA's error
(results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json,
results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json). Seeing a geometry at another angle
helps the 35-case constant-gauge ISLA by 15%
(results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json).

*Flow difficulty.* On the 35-case random split the constant-gauge ISLA's
error is 0.09–0.10 in attached flow (4°–12°) and 0.17–0.19 post-stall, it
interpolates smoothly at the one angle (18°) absent from training (0.135 →
0.167 → 0.186 across 16°, 18° and 20°), and its per-case coefficient of
variation is 0.44 at 35 cases and 0.64 at 210, rising with angle of attack
(rank correlation 0.56 and 0.61) and not with how far a case's field is
from uniform (results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json,
results/hilift_error_drivers_2026-09-07.json). Its residual error
concentrates where the geometry is intricate: 59% of its squared pressure
error at 35 cases, and 71% at 210, falls on the 15% of points within 2% of
chord of a facing surface, the slat and flap gaps (@tbl-hilift-hlreg).
Against reference predictors on the same cases (constant freestream
pressure 1.00 on the gauge-pressure scale, dataset mean 0.94, per-case mean
0.93) it scores 0.25, with a median per-case correlation of 0.97 between
predicted and true pressure
(results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json; this analysis uses
the gauge-pressure scale, on which 0.25 corresponds to 0.138 on the recipe
metric).

| training cases | near band (0.7–2% chord), about 15% of points | 2–10% of chord, about 6% of points | open surface (>10%), about 79% of points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | 59% | 4% | 36% |
| 210 | 71% | 4% | 23% |

: Where ISLA's residual pressure error lives on the 35- and 210-case
random splits (constant-gauge variant, two-seed mean predictions, median
over the 180 validation cases): the share of ISLA's own squared error that
falls in each facing-surface-distance band, with the median share of the
10,000 sampled points that each band holds. The facing-surface distance is
the distance from a sampled point to the nearest boundary-mesh vertex in
front of the surface within 10% of chord, which is the local gap or cove
width and is infinite on an open convex surface (@sec-nb-hlreg-amendment).
Data:
results/hlreg_facing_distance_35_2026-09-08.json,
results/hlreg_facing_distance_210_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-hilift-hlreg}

*Capacity.* Trained and evaluated on one case at a time (64 sampled views of
a single wing, float32 at 10,000 cells), ISLA's floor is 1.27x
GeoTransolver's and 1.37x Transolver's, wider than the 35-case gap of
1.11–1.20x, and the deficit sits on the smooth, large-cell open surfaces
(baseline ÷ ISLA 0.64–0.83) rather than at the gaps (0.88). A deficit that
widens when the data are held fixed is not a data limit; it is
representational, visible in ISLA's own training losses
(results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json; @sec-nb-overfit-verdict).

## In engineering terms: lift and drag {#sec-de-forces}

Integrating the predicted pressure and wall shear over each wing gives its
lift and drag coefficients. From 35 CFD runs the constant-gauge ISLA
predicts the drag coefficient of the 180 validation cases to 3.3% and the
lift coefficient to 3.0% (mean absolute error relative to the mean
magnitude of the reference coefficient), and from 1,260 to 1.4% and 0.9%
(results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json). The reference is the CFD
label integrated on the *same* 10,000 sampled cells as the prediction
(@sec-metrics): the errors are against that sampled-cell integral, not the
full-surface force, and because prediction and label share the quadrature,
the sampling error of a 10,000-cell integral cancels in them. How far a
10,000-cell integral sits from the full-surface force is not measured
(@sec-program-status). The unit-drive baselines' force coefficients are not
reduced, so no force comparison between architectures is made; the 3%
figure says that a few-dozen-run design-of-experiments budget yields a
force surrogate of usable accuracy from ISLA, not that ISLA is the only
architecture that delivers one.

## A free uncertainty signal {#sec-de-uq}

The disagreement between a model's two seeds ranks its per-case error: for
the constant-gauge ISLA at 35 cases the Spearman correlation between
two-seed disagreement and per-case error over the 180 validation cases is
+0.67, at 210 cases about +0.6, and at 1,260 cases +0.15, where seed
disagreement no longer predicts error (@sec-shared-floor). Two-seed
ensembles gain only 1–5% at any rung, and only the ranking is tested, not
calibration.^[`results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{35,210,1260}_2026-09-06.json`.]
A two-seed ISLA therefore ships with a usable per-case confidence flag from
35 cases. The same signal is not measured for the unit-drive baselines, so
no comparison with them is made.

## What each ingredient costs ISLA {#sec-mechanism}

ISLA differs from the Transolver family in several ways at once: exact
rotation and translation equivariance, an invariant seed parameterization,
measure-weighted routing, equivariant slice anchors with relational
invariants, and an optional similarity gauge. Removing one at a time from
the constant-gauge variant at 35 cases (error 0.138) gives:

| single-factor change to the constant-gauge ISLA at 35 cases | error (seed 42 / 43) | vs 0.138 |
|---|---|---|
| add raw coordinates as inputs (breaks exact equivariance) | 0.143 / 0.143 | 1.04x |
| replace the invariant seeds by the raw vectors [r, n, d] | 0.138 / 0.137 | 0.99x |
| similarity gauge on | 0.151 / 0.147 | 1.08x |
| measure weights off (ablation, not adopted) | 0.121 / 0.123 | **0.88x** |
| relational routing off in the encoder | 0.158 / 0.163 | 1.16x |

: Single-factor ablations of ISLA's constant-gauge variant at 35 training cases, two seeds, frozen protocol, shared validation set. Every variant retains an invariant path somewhere (the relational invariants in the encoder, or in the decoder read blocks), so these results speak to exactness and to individual ingredients, not to the presence of invariant information. Data: results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-ablations}

No single ingredient moves ISLA's error by more than 16%. Exactness of the
equivariance is not load-bearing in distribution (adding raw coordinates
costs 4%); the invariant seed set is not (raw vectors cost nothing); the
similarity gauge costs 8% at this rung; relational routing is worth 16%.

**Measure weights are a correctness requirement, and their in-distribution
price on the wings is known.** Turning them off improves the constant-gauge
ISLA by 12% at 35 cases (5–10% across draws), 8% at 210, 17% at 4
geometries, 11% at 21 and 11% at the fixed angle, and by 3% on DrivAerML
(results/nowl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json,
results/now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json). The price has two parts. One is
estimator variance: with weights on, the effective number of tokens per
slice is about a fifth of the count (540 against 2,030 on a wing sample,
because 4.4% of the cells carry half the area), and on DrivAerML the
weights-off advantage shrinks from 11% at 2,500 cells to 2.4% at 40,000
(@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe). The other is mesh-pattern content: on the
wings the advantage is flat at 12–13% from 2,500 to 40,000 cells, which
variance cannot be, and under area-proportional resampling it inverts 2–7x,
the weights-off model's absolute error rising to 0.66–1.29, worse than
predicting zero, while the weighted model's falls with count
(@sec-nb-bench-verdict). A configuration that reads the mesher's cell
placement is not a surrogate for the surface (@sec-principle); the
weights-off ISLA is an ablation, reported wherever it prices the measure
semantics, and never a configuration.

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

There is no ISLA advantage on DrivAerML at any training-set size. Its
data-efficiency ladder (@sec-datasets) trains both architectures on nested
subsets of the 435-car training split, 14, 27, 54, 109 and 218 cars, under
the frozen protocol of that ladder, learning rate 3e-3 for both, 500
epochs, 10,000 tokens, two seeds, scored on the 48-car validation split.
GeoTransolver's DrivAerML ladder lanes received the freestream as a
physical velocity of 38.9 m/s; at 435 cars the unit-drive GeoTransolver
scores 0.0503 against 0.0498 in float32, inside the null band, so on this
dataset the input scale is not a handicap and the ladder ordering is read
as it stands (@sec-nb-uw-verdict, @sec-nb-fp32-drivaer-regrade).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "ladder_reduction.json"))
print("| training cars | GeoTransolver | ISLA, constant-gauge variant | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for n in (14, 27, 54, 109, 218):
    g = [lad[f"lad_gt_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    m = [lad[f"lad_mt2_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    print(f"| {n} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {mm:.3f} ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} |")
print()
print(": DrivAerML data-efficiency ladder: surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 validation cars, seed mean (seed range), at learning rate 3e-3 for both architectures (the frozen protocol of that ladder; ISLA's preferred rate of 1e-3 is worth about 1.1x at full data and does not change the ordering). ISLA is the constant-gauge variant; the reference configuration is trained on DrivAerML only at 435 cars (@sec-full-data-accuracy). GT / ISLA below one means GeoTransolver is more accurate. bfloat16 evaluation on identical points; the float32 offset on this dataset (@sec-metrics) moves every close comparison toward GeoTransolver. Data: results/ladder_reduction.json. {#tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder}")
```

At 14 cars the two architectures tie at 0.27; from 27 cars up GeoTransolver
is 1.2–1.3x more accurate, and at the full 435 cars, in float32,
GeoTransolver scores 0.0503 and Transolver 0.0517 against 0.0552 for ISLA's
reference configuration (@sec-full-data-accuracy). The same ordering holds
on the interior: GeoTransolver's volume configuration leads ISLA's
query-token configuration on interior pressure by about 1.2x at 54 and 109
cars and by 7% at 435, where ISLA leads on velocity by 1.37x
(@sec-interior). On DrivAerML the surface deficit is uniform in every way
measured: the same on every third of the car (@sec-limits-mechanism), a
near-constant factor per car on a difficulty ordering both architectures
share (per-case rank correlation 0.86–0.89, equal to each architecture's
correlation with its own second seed;
results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json), unchanged by a wider
ISLA at the reference cell count, and the same for the surface and the
volume.

## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

**The comparison is only as fair as its inputs, and the protocol says so.**
Every input each architecture receives is listed with its scale, the scales
are matched across architectures, and a control that varies only an input
is part of the steel-man set before any ratio is stated (@sec-protocol).
The freestream enters every model as a unit direction; the alternative is
the documented hazard of @sec-part-baseline.

**The ladder is a data-efficiency measurement, not a scaling law.** The
constant-gauge ISLA's log-log slopes of error against training cases
flatten from 0.42 to 0.31 to 0.21 over the 35→210, 210→510 and 510→1,260
segments; the baselines' curves are measured to 510 cases and are flat in
ratio to ISLA's. The book makes no claim beyond 1,260 cases. Three pieces
of evidence suggest the flattening is a floor of the protocol rather than a
property of ISLA: 70% of the residual at full data is shared between
architectures on identical points, the seed-disagreement correlation
collapses for both at 1,260 cases, and accuracy still rises with tokens
per case. That reading is a hypothesis, not a result (@sec-shared-floor).

**It is one dataset, and on the other the ordering is the same.** On
DrivAerML GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 training cars up
and the two tie at 14 (@sec-de-drivaerml); on HiLiftAeroML the baselines
lead by 12–32% on every rung measured. No dataset in this book shows an
in-distribution accuracy advantage for ISLA at any training-set size.

**It is in-distribution, and it is a validation-set figure.** The
validation cases are random draws from the same 180-geometry, ten-angle
design as the training cases (180 cases on 118 geometries); the checkpoints
are final-epoch, with no selection on validation error, but the validation
set was reused adaptively (the baselines' learning rate per rung, the
ablations designed after earlier readouts, the choice of what to present),
and the sealed test split has been spent on regime extrapolation and one
mechanism test, so no held-out evaluation of the small-data models exists.
Nor can one be an independent confirmation at the level of the program: the
regime-extrapolation test sets cover all 180 geometries and share 179 of
the 360 data-efficiency test cases, so a later evaluation on that manifest
would be held out per checkpoint but not unexposed (@sec-limits-validation).
What happens across a regime boundary is the subject of
@sec-regime-extrapolation, and the answer there is that no architecture
generalizes.

**Seeds do not measure the choice of training cases.** Every seed at a rung
trains on the same curated subset, so the seed spread measures
initialization and data order, not which 35 cases a practitioner would
happen to have; the draw intervals of @sec-de-result are the uncertainty to
read, and they are measured only at 35 and 210 cases.

**No mechanism of an ISLA accuracy advantage is established, because no
ISLA accuracy advantage over an input-matched baseline is established.** The
single-factor ablations of @tbl-hilift-ablations price ISLA's ingredients
against ISLA's own reference (no ingredient worth more than 16%); the
single-case study of @sec-de-strata locates the deficit in capacity on
smooth open surfaces. What ISLA buys is stated elsewhere: exact pose
covariance (@sec-pose-contract), a frame that carries no mesher information
and converges under refinement (@sec-consistency-bench), and the interior
velocity lead (@sec-interior).
